source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Asking a model to review its own answer, with no outside label, lowers accuracy. The model changes right answers to wrong ones more often than the reverse.
numbers: GPT-4 intrinsic self-correction: GSM8K 95.5 (standard) to 91.5 (round 1) to 89.0 (round 2); CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 79.5 to 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 49.0 to 43.0. GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 to 41.8. GPT-3.5 kept its first answer 74.7% of the time on GSM8K; of the rest, more correct-to-incorrect than incorrect-to-correct.
quote: LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning
limits: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo, Llama-2 (2023 models), not modern reasoning models. Figure percentages for the flip classes were garbled in text extraction, so only the direction is recorded.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a first-answer-then-verify step with the same model is not free. It needs a measured flip rate on our own model, and should only overwrite an answer on outside evidence.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (oracle-label analysis)
finding: Reported self-correction gains come from using ground-truth labels to decide when to stop. Without labels the gains vanish.
numbers: With oracle labels (stop when correct) self-correction raised scores; without them every benchmark and model dropped (Tables 3 to 6, several prompts).
limits: Oracle stopping is not available at deployment. Same 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a verify step only helps if it carries real outside signal (tests, tools, a second source), not the model's own opinion.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam and Kambhampati (2024) On the Self-Verification Limitations of LLMs on Reasoning and Planning Tasks
finding: GPT-4 as its own verifier makes results worse on Game of 24 and Graph Coloring. A sound external verifier gives large gains. Re-prompting alone with a sound verifier keeps most of the gain.
numbers: Success rates, standard prompt / LLM+LLM backprompt / LLM+sound verifier (best format) / sampling k=25: Game of 24 5/3/38/42; Graph Coloring 16/2/38/44; Blocksworld 40/55/87/72; Mystery Blocksworld 4/0/10/14. Game of 24 verifier: false positive 10.4% (320/3071), false negative 20.7% (213/1029) as read from Table 2 (column order inferred). Of correct equations it marked 79.1% correct but evaluated 81.6% as equal to 24.
limits: One model (GPT-4, 2024). Table 2 text was garbled in extraction so some cell-to-column mappings are inferred. Blocksworld shows a modest self-critique gain (40 to 55).
agent_relevance: Gap 3: yes, self-verification can turn correct answers into rejected ones (high false-negative rate, then timeout on worse generations). Verification must be external or rule-based; this matches the human point that System 2 monitoring is unreliable.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs
finding: A survey of the self-correction literature finds no prior work showing successful self-correction with feedback from a prompted LLM, except on tasks unusually suited to it. It works well with reliable external feedback and with large-scale fine-tuning.
numbers: Three findings in the abstract: (1) no demonstrated prompted self-correction except suited tasks; (2) works with reliable external feedback; (3) fine-tuning enables it. Bottleneck named as feedback generation.
limits: Survey up to 2024. Does not test 2025-26 reasoning models trained with RL, which may self-check better.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: supports a rule in the schema: verification steps use tools or independent evidence; same-model re-reading is not counted as a check. Modern RL-trained models remain untested here, so the gap is only partly closed.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs
finding: Verbalised confidence is overconfident and a weak failure detector. Agreement across several sampled answers is a much better signal than a stated number.
numbers: Five models, eight datasets. GPT-4 vanilla verbalised confidence: average AUROC 62.7% (random is 50%). GSM8K: AUROC 54.8% with verbalised confidence vs 92.7% with 5-sample consistency aggregation. White-box vs black-box gap 0.522 to 0.605 AUROC. GPT-4 GSM8K accuracy 93.6%; it got near-optimal ECE 0.064 by giving 100% confidence to all items, which is useless for ranking.
limits: Models 2023 (GPT-3, 3.5, 4, Vicuna, Llama 2). Weak on professional-knowledge tasks. Not a test of the human conflict-detection confidence drop.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 4: a stated-confidence trigger for 'go slow' is unreliable. Use sample disagreement (cheap when answers are short) as the trigger. An ECE number alone can hide a constant-confidence model.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration: Strategies for Eliciting Calibrated Confidence Scores from Language Models Fine-Tuned with Human Feedback
finding: For RLHF chat models (ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude 2), words-as-output confidence is better calibrated than the token probability, often cutting expected calibration error by a relative 50%.
numbers: TriviaQA, SciQ, TruthfulQA. Relative ECE reduction over 50% with verbalised confidence vs conditional probabilities. Asking for several answer options first (considering the opposite) improved calibration further.
limits: Trivia-style knowledge questions only; calibration measured on average, not on conflict items. Raw logit probabilities of RLHF models are over-confident.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: after instruction tuning, verbalised confidence is calibrated on average (Tian) yet separates right from wrong poorly (Xiong). Calibrated on average is not the same as a usable trigger. No study reproduces the human De Neys confidence drop specifically on conflict items; that part stays open.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context
finding: Irrelevant sentences cut arithmetic accuracy sharply. Adding the single instruction 'Feel free to ignore irrelevant information' in one pass restores about as much as showing distractor-bearing examples. Self-consistency adds more.
numbers: GSM-IC-4K on code-davinci-002. Self-consistency (20 samples) improved micro accuracy by more than 11 points overall and 35.5 points for zero-shot CoT; correct answer was among 20 samples for 99.7% of problems (96.5% for 0-CoT). Best macro accuracy still only 45%. On clean GSM8K dev, instruction did not hurt (CoT 59.3 vs 60.3 with instruction).
quote: Feel free to ignore irrelevant information given in the questions.
limits: 2022-2023 model; irrelevant-sentence arithmetic only. Not a head-to-head with System 2 Attention (which used LLaMA-2-70B: 80.3 vs 71.7).
agent_relevance: Gap 5: partly closed. A one-line instruction is a cheap single-pass baseline that must be beaten before paying for a context-rewrite pass. No equal-token comparison on a current frontier model was found.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 failed all three CRT items with the intuitive answer. On slight rewrites of heuristics-and-biases vignettes its answers changed a lot, which the authors read as possible training-set exposure plus brittleness.
numbers: 12 vignettes: 6 correct, all 12 human-like. CRT1-CRT3: intuitive wrong answer on all 3. Variants: a CRT item with the wrong premise ('bat costs $1.00 more than the bat') still gave $0.10; reordering Wason options (4, 7, A, K) changed the answer to turn A and K; the cab problem with 'black' cab gave 20%.
limits: GPT-3 (text-davinci-002) only. Perturbed items were a handful of hand-made probes, not a systematic benchmark. Frontier models now solve the CRT (see K08), so these failures are outdated for them.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: contamination is real for famous items. Any evaluation of our agent on CRT-like traps must use rewritten items with new surface and new numbers; a score on the original wording says little.

source: Liang et al. (2025) ThinkSwitcher: When to Think Hard, When to Think Fast
finding: A small trained switch picks short or long chain of thought per question. It cut tokens 20 to 30% with 1 to 2 points lower average accuracy than always-long. A BERT classifier router saved more tokens on the 1.5B model but with a large accuracy loss.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B, 7B, 14B on seven math benchmarks. 14B macro average: ThinkSwitcher 66.9 accuracy with 5,603 tokens vs BERT router 65.0 with 5,983. Over 30% token saving on 1.5B.
limits: Math only. Trained router needs labelled data. Compares at chosen thresholds, not at equal total tokens, so no study here fixes a token budget and tests routed vs fixed arms at the same cost.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: routing roughly keeps accuracy at lower cost; mis-routing shows up as accuracy loss on the BERT arm (about 2 points average at 14B plus larger drops at 1.5B). The equal-token test is still not run.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) SynapseRoute: An Auto-Route Switching Framework on Dual-State LLM
finding: On medical questions, about 58% can be answered correctly without thinking. A learned router beat thinking-mode-always on accuracy while using fewer tokens. Over-reasoning on easy items sometimes lowered accuracy.
numbers: Accuracy: thinking mode 0.8272, non-thinking 0.5774, SynapseRoute 0.8390. Inference time down 36.8%, tokens down 39.66% versus thinking mode.
limits: Medical benchmarks only; vendor model; single paper. Not matched on tokens, only reports savings. The gain of 1.2 points is small.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 2: router can beat both extremes on accuracy per token on a mixed set, but where the cost of mis-routing falls is not isolated. Task-class router (medical question complexity) is a cheaper signal than model confidence.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Adaptive Dual Reasoner: Large Reasoning Models Can Think Efficiently by Hybrid Reasoning
finding: A model trained to switch between fast and slow reasoning inside one chain cut output length about half with equal or higher accuracy on maths.
numbers: Up to 6.1% performance gain; reasoning output length reduced 49.5% to 59.3%.
limits: Trained model (SFT plus RL), math only. Only abstract and introduction were read, not the result tables.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: in-chain switching is said to beat coarse per-question routing; it is learned, which an agent without training cannot copy.

source: Han et al. (2025) Token-Budget-Aware LLM Reasoning (TALE)
finding: Putting a token budget in the prompt cuts chain-of-thought length. Models overshoot too-small budgets, so cutting the budget further can raise actual token use. A per-question estimated budget kept accuracy.
numbers: TALE-EP: 67% average token reduction with under 3% accuracy decrease. TALE-PT: about 50% fewer tokens than vanilla CoT. Example: with a 50-token budget the model used 157 tokens, about twice as many as with a larger budget.
limits: Budget is a prompt request, not a hard cutoff; this is a length-compression study, not a time-pressure manipulation with a human analogue.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: a token budget does not behave like human time pressure. Humans are forced to stop; LLMs may ignore the limit ('token elasticity'), so only a hard cap on generation tests the analogue.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? (sampling and aggregation)
finding: More sampled responses improve failure prediction and then level off. Consistency among answers works best on arithmetic.
numbers: 5 samples with consistency aggregation lifted GSM8K AUROC from 54.8% to 92.7%; performance improves with number of samples then converges (Figure 7).
limits: Costs M times the tokens, so against a single slow pass it is not equal-token.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a direct-vs-CoT or sample disagreement check is the best cheap predictor found, but it is not tested for predicting CoT harm specifically.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context (self-consistency recall)
finding: Even when single answers are distracted, the correct answer is nearly always somewhere in the sampled set, so selection, not generation, is the weak step.
numbers: Correct answer in 20 samples: 99.7% (CoT and LTM), 96.5% (0-CoT); but macro accuracy of the best method only 45%.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 5: supports sampling plus independent selection over the model re-reading its own work.

source: Stechly et al. (2024) self-verification: sound verifier keeps most gains
finding: With a sound verifier, even bare re-prompting keeps most of the gain; the content of the critique matters little.
numbers: Game of 24: sampling k=25 reached 42% against 38% for best critique format; Graph Coloring 44% vs 38%; Mystery Blocksworld 14% vs 10%.
limits: GPT-4 only; tasks with exact verifiers.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the useful ingredient is the checker, not the reflective text. Spend tokens on a checker or extra samples.

source: Frederick (2005) Cognitive Reflection and Decision Making; Evans et al. (1983); Hagger et al. (2016); Bago and De Neys (2017): founding-number check
finding: Not verified. Direct download of Frederick's paper returned a web page, not the PDF; Evans 1983, Hagger 2016 and Bago and De Neys 2017 were not reachable open access in this session. Search APIs were rate limited (HTTP 429) so no mirror was found.
limits: Gap 7 stays open. Do not quote per-site CRT means, belief-bias percentages, ego-depletion d, or the 90% two-response figure as checked.
agent_relevance: Treat these numbers as unverified background until a PDF is read.
